blocks.text: BLEU, bilingual evaluation understudy, is one of the oldest automated metrics for scoring generated text against a reference, originally built for machine translation and still widely reported as a quick, cheap proxy for output quality.
This topic covers how BLEU actually computes its score, what it is good at capturing, and where it falls short as a signal for evaluating fine-tuned language models.

BLEU scores how much overlapping word sequences a generated candidate shares with one or more human written reference texts, producing a single number that is meant to approximate how close a machine output is to acceptable human quality.

Rather than checking single word overlap alone, BLEU checks matching sequences of one, two, three, and four consecutive words, called n-grams, since matching longer sequences is a stronger signal of genuine fluency than matching isolated words scattered across the text.

code.content:
from collections import Counter

def ngram_precision(candidate_tokens, reference_tokens, n):
    cand_ngrams = Counter(tuple(candidate_tokens[i:i+n]) for i in range(len(candidate_tokens)-n+1))
    ref_ngrams = Counter(tuple(reference_tokens[i:i+n]) for i in range(len(reference_tokens)-n+1))
    matched = sum(min(count, ref_ngrams[gram]) for gram, count in cand_ngrams.items())
    total = sum(cand_ngrams.values())
    return matched / total if total else 0.0

blocks.text: 3. Turning Matches Into a Precision Score

blocks.alt: Turning Matches Into a Precision Score

blocks.text: For each n-gram length, BLEU computes a precision, the fraction of candidate n-grams that also appear in the reference, then combines precision scores across all four n-gram lengths, typically using a geometric mean, into a single combined precision figure.

Precision alone rewards short outputs unfairly, since a very short candidate can achieve high precision just by containing only words that happen to appear in the reference, BLEU corrects for this with a brevity penalty that reduces the score when a candidate is noticeably shorter than the reference.

blocks.text: BLEU tends to work reasonably well for tasks with a fairly narrow range of acceptable outputs, machine translation, where the reference translation and a good candidate translation genuinely do share a lot of overlapping word sequences.

Because BLEU only credits exact word sequence matches, a candidate that is a genuinely good, fluent paraphrase of the reference, using entirely different words, scores poorly, a real weakness for open ended generation tasks like summarization, dialogue, or creative writing, where many different phrasings can all be equally correct.

blocks.title: BLEU rewards surface overlap, not meaning
blocks.content: A candidate response that says something semantically identical to the reference using different words receives little credit under BLEU, since the metric has no concept of meaning, only literal word sequence matching.

blocks.text: ROUGE, covered in the next topic, shares BLEU n-gram overlap foundation but flips the emphasis toward recall rather than precision, making the two metrics complementary rather than interchangeable, BLEU is traditionally reported for translation, ROUGE for summarization.
8. BLEU in a Fine-Tuning Evaluation Pipeline

When evaluating a fine-tuned model, BLEU is best used as one fast, cheap signal among several, useful for catching regressions during rapid iteration, but rarely sufficient on its own to judge whether a model output is genuinely good, especially for tasks with more than one valid correct answer.

BLEU scores are sensitive to tokenization choices, the number of reference texts available, and n-gram length settings, comparisons across different papers or pipelines using inconsistent BLEU implementations can be misleading, using a standardized implementation matters more than it might first appear.

A team fine-tuning a translation model computes BLEU on a held out test set after each training checkpoint, watching the score rise from 18 to 31 over several epochs, a useful quick signal that the model is learning the target language pair.

When they later apply the same fine-tuning pipeline to a dialogue generation task, BLEU scores stay stubbornly low even as human reviewers rate the outputs as clearly improving, a mismatch that reveals BLEU is the wrong primary metric for that particular task and prompts them to add human evaluation, covered in an earlier topic, as the primary signal instead.

items: Using BLEU as the sole evaluation metric for open ended generation tasks where many valid phrasings exist
Comparing BLEU scores computed with different tokenization or reference set choices as if they were directly comparable
Forgetting that a low BLEU score does not necessarily mean a bad output, it may mean a valid paraphrase
Ignoring the brevity penalty and being misled by an artificially short candidate output

blocks.text: Take one reference sentence and write two different candidate sentences, one that closely repeats the reference wording and one that says the same thing in genuinely different words, then reason through by hand which one BLEU would likely score higher and why.

BLEU scores generated text by n-gram overlap against a reference, adjusted with a brevity penalty, a metric that works reasonably well for tasks with a narrow range of acceptable outputs like translation, but struggles to fairly credit valid paraphrases, making it a useful but insufficient signal for evaluating open ended fine-tuned model outputs on its own.
